articles.title: I Watched Smoke Signals For The First Time, And Two Things Really Caught Me Off Guard
articles.summary: I expected a road trip comedy and got so much more.
articles.content:
Amid the various kinds of films I enjoy, coming-of-age movies hold a special place in my heart. There’s something special about a story that sees young people navigating growing pains, whether they be Black-led coming-of-age stories or those told from other perspectives. On that note, I had been meaning to watch the much revered Smoke Signals for some time, and I finally did that amid Native American Heritage Month. I’m pleased to say that not only is the movie great as promised, but it also surprised me in two ways.

Released in 1998, Smoke Signals is based on screenwriter Sherman Alexie’s The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven . The Chris Eyre-directed road trip dramedy primarily centers around two Indigenous teens – Victor Joseph (Adam Beach) and Thomas Builds-the-Fire (Evan Adams). The mismatched pair set off on a trip from their Idaho-based reservation to Phoenix, Arizona, to collect the ashes of Victor’s recently deceased father.

Alcoholism is also explored in great depth, as flashbacks show both of the Arnolds dealing with it, to the point where a young Victor destroys their beer in defiance. It’s a striking moment and serves as the wake-up call Victor’s mother, Arlene (Tantoo Cardinal), needs. Additionally, domestic abuse is a key theme, as Arnold is shown abusing Victor and Arlene on different occasions. Overall, through the Josephs, audiences get a nuanced look at dysfunctional intergenerational relationships .

Smoke Signals also has other grim moments. I mean, the film opens with a flashback to the night of a Fourth of July party, at which point Thomas’ parents are killed in a house fire. And the only reason baby Thomas survives is due to being saved by Arnold, who Thomas grows to idolize despite his faults. While the darker material caught me off guard, I truly appreciated Eyre and Alexie tackling such subject matter and doing so with some layered Indigenous characters .

Throughout the film, there’s also a heavy emphasis on the Native American tradition of oral storytelling. Much of that is thanks to Thomas, who tells stories – that vary in terms of how true they are – whether people want to hear them or not. Adams delivers these soliloquies perfectly, and they add a soulful element to the film. I particularly love when Thomas bonds over storytelling with Arnold’s Phoenix- based friend, Suzy Song (Irene Bedard), who is a badass Indigenous woman in a fairly understated way.

All in all, this keen focus on storytelling only enhances the movie, and Eyre and Alexie’s reverence for it is more than evident. It also opens the door for viewers like myself to gain a better understanding of an aspect of Native American culture we wouldn’t otherwise be privy to. As a viewer, I really enjoy being engulfed in different cultural perspectives via film and TV, and truly relish whenever nuanced stories centered on (and told by) Indigenous people are pushed to the forefront.

articles.title: 'The Tree' Director Julie Bertuccelli Tells IFFI Masterclass a Canadian Producer Stole Her 'Italian Shoes' Adaptation, Readies India-Set Feature
articles.summary: French filmmaker Julie Bertuccelli, whose "The Tree" closed the Cannes Film Festival in 2010, said her planned adaptation of Henning Mankell's novel "Italian Shoes" fell apart after a Canadian producer "stole the film" from her, and that she plans to shoot her next feature in India. Bertuccelli was speaking at "From Witness to Change: The […]
articles.content:
French filmmaker Julie Bertuccelli , whose "The Tree" closed the Cannes Film Festival in 2010, said her planned adaptation of Henning Mankell's novel "Italian Shoes" fell apart after a Canadian producer "stole the film" from her, and that she plans to shoot her next feature in India.

Bertuccelli was speaking at "From Witness to Change: The Social Responsibility of Documentary Cinema," a masterclass at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, moderated by Indian filmmaker Haobam Paban Kumar. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Ji.hlava New Visions Award Winner Karim Akalay Mixes Magic With ‘Anti-Social Realism’ in ‘6TM’: ‘It’s About Collective Strength Rather Than One Hero’ Alex Gibney-Produced ‘Mohabat,’ Directed by James Longley, Wins at Ji.hlava: The Film Is 'Meticulously Researched and Exquisitely Crafted'

Responding to an audience question, Bertuccelli said she set out to adapt the Mankell book five years ago. She wrote the script and cast the film, which was due to shoot in Canada, before the pandemic brought everything to a halt.

"In fact there is a bad Canadian producer who stole the film from me," Bertuccelli said. She did not name the producer and declined to give the full account. She said she was forced to cancel the project, adding: "I worked for quite four years, five years for nothing because they stole from me, they stole, you know, the movie and I could not do it. So it was very hard."

Bertuccelli turned to the directors in the room. "It's a fight against you, against yourself, because you need to work, you need even when you are depressed or you have doubts, you need to continue, because the only thing that makes you a director is that you go on and you never, you know, you never stop your desire," she said.

She is now writing the new feature. It follows a French woman living in Mumbai who is slowly going blind and sets off on one last journey with her son, who is half Indian and half French. Bertuccelli plans to come to India to make it. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"It's my first time in India, but for so long I'm admiring your country, your culture," she said.

Bertuccelli is also finishing a second documentary alongside "The Violin Lesson," which follows Rachel Routier, a violin teacher in Pantin, outside Paris, and is headed for French cinemas after airing on France Télévisions in September. She hopes to screen "The Violin Lesson" in Mumbai in the coming weeks, along with either "The Tree" or "Since Otar Left."

During two terms as president of La Scam, the French authors' society for documentary makers, Bertuccelli created the Golden Eye documentary prize at Cannes, whose Indian winners include Payal Kapadia's "A Night of Knowing Nothing" and Shaunak Sen's "All That Breathes." She also founded La Cinémathèque du documentaire in Paris, which hopes to stage a retrospective of Indian documentary.

Asked by Kumar whether documentary carries a social responsibility, Bertuccelli said: "For sure there is a big responsibility because the film can change the life of somebody, you know?"

She pointed to "School of Babel," which followed a class for children newly arrived in France. The film was widely seen by school groups and shifted young viewers' attitudes toward immigrant classmates, she said, and it helped protect such classes at a time when some were being closed. "Because I said with this film to all the Education Ministry: 'So I made a film to show that France is great, but don't touch it. Now you can't destroy this,'" she said.

Kumar later asked where cinema stands in the age of AI. Bertuccelli allowed that the technology can be useful for small tasks, such as sound work.

"But I hate AI. Not just because, okay, it's dangerous for us, we will forget how to have memory, how to think by ourselves. Also because they steal, they stole the film, you know, they stole the author rights. But also more because it's an ecological, horrible, horrible thing," she said.

Documentary, she argued, is cinema's last line of defense, because "there is a contract with you that when you see a documentary, there is reality, there is truth." She added that "the 21st century will be the one of documentary."

Bertuccelli spent around 15 years as an assistant to directors including Krzysztof Kieślowski, Bertrand Tavernier and Otar Iosseliani before making her own documentaries. Her fiction debut, "Since Otar Left," shot in Georgia, won the Critics' Week grand prize at Cannes and the César for best first film. Her documentary work includes "School of Babel," "Latest News From the Cosmos" and "Jane Campion, the Cinema Woman." "The Tree," starring Charlotte Gainsbourg, played IFFI more than 15 years ago, but Bertuccelli could not attend as she was eight months pregnant at the time. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

She closed the session by pointing back to the Lumière brothers, whose operators traveled the world filming everyday life.

"Cinema was born documentary and it will die documentary," she said.

articles.content:
The life and legacy of legendary Egyptian artist Mohamed Mounir is set to be explored in a biopic spearheaded by The Film Committee at Media City Qatar .

The Film Committee has acquired the rights to document Mounir’s life story, with partners on the project set to include a leading regional studio and other partners, which have yet to be announced.

His 1981 breakthrough album ‘Shababeek’ established him as one of Egypt ’s most distinctive artists, with his work characterized by its fusion of Nubian folk and Arabic pop with Western genres like jazz, blues, and reggae.

He is known to his fans across the Middle East and beyond as “El King” in reference to his 1998 album and play ‘El Malek Howwa El Malek’ ((The King is The King).

Also working in cinema, his some 20 credits including collaborations with late Egyptian filmmaker Youssef Chahine on films including Egyptian Story (1982) and Destiny, which played in Out of Competition in Cannes in 1997 and was then selected as Egypt’s Oscar entry.

Mounir was born into a Nubian family in a village in Southern Egypt, where he spent his early childhood. His family moved to Cairo, after the village was resettled due to the construction of the Aswan Dam in the 1960s, where his singing voice was discovered when he sang at a family gathering.

The Film Committee said the biopic will trace Mounir's journey from his humble beginnings to becoming one of the Arab world’s most celebrated and influential artists, revealing untold details, surprises, stories and anecdotes.

“Mohamed Mounir’s music holds a special place in the lives of audiences across Egypt and the Arab world,” said Film Committee at Media City Qatar Chair Hassan Al Thawadi. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“ Bringing his story to the big screen is an opportunity to celebrate his artistry, the cultural heritage his work represents and its lasting social relevance, a story that connects generations of fans across the region and has the power to resonate with audiences around the world," he continued.

“This project also builds on our recent investment in extraordinary life stories from the region and reflects our ambition to develop a world-leading slate of biographical films that brings these stories to audiences globally.”

Alongside the feature film, plans include a behind-the-scenes documentary featuring interviews with Mounir and those who have lived and worked alongside him, as well as documenting the development and production of the biopic.

With development in the early stages, the hunt is now on for an actor to play Mounir.

The Qatar Film Committee is an official body that is part of the Media City Qatar hub and is tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry.

Founded in April 2024 by brothers Badie Ali and Hamza Ali, Chicago-based Watermelon Pictures has gained worldwide attention in its short time in business with releases such as Rashid Masharawi's "From Ground Zero," Annemarie Jacir's "Palestine 36" and Cherien Dabis' "All That’s Left of You," which were shortlisted for the best international feature Oscar, as well as Kaouther ben Hania's Oscar-nominated "The Voice of Hind Rajab."

The partnership between Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon was announced on the second day of the Doha Film Festival ’s Industry Days, which are running from Nov. 19-21.

"Combining Qatar's commitment to world-class filmmaking, growing production capabilities, and investment in the creative economy with Watermelon's access to leading talent, established distribution infrastructure, and deep understanding of what resonates with audiences, the collaboration aims to produce commercially compelling films with high production values and international appeal," the statement said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The plan envisions that these projects will shoot mainly in Qatar or be structured as Qatari co-productions. They will tap into the country’s growing production ecosystem and the Qatar Screen Production Incentive rebate offering up to 50% in cash, "creating opportunities for local crews, businesses and creative talent while strengthening Qatar's position as an international production hub," it noted.

“Through this partnership, we want to give filmmakers the resources to tell stories rooted in their communities and bring them to audiences around the world," Hassan Al Thawadi, the Qatari lawyer who chairs the Qatar Film Committee, said in the statement.

articles.title: Indian Auteur Girish Kasaravalli Looks Back on 50 Years of Cinema at IFFI Masterclass: 'All My Films Talk About Othering'
articles.summary: Indian auteur Girish Kasaravalli looked back on his career in Kannada-language cinema at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, in a masterclass titled "The Moral Universe of Parallel Cinema: 50 Years of Girish Kasaravalli." The 75-year-old spoke about the moral contradictions of society and the relationship between cinematic form and social […]
articles.content:
Indian auteur Girish Kasaravalli looked back on his career in Kannada-language cinema at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, in a masterclass titled "The Moral Universe of Parallel Cinema: 50 Years of Girish Kasaravalli."

The 75-year-old spoke about the moral contradictions of society and the relationship between cinematic form and social content. He also argued that even entertainment is a political act. The session was moderated by Variety 's Asia editor Naman Ramachandran. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Margot Robbie to Star in A24's 'The Week of Pain' From 'The Drama' Director Kristoffer Borgli Jo Koy on ‘Blue in the Face,’ Steven Spielberg, Biggie’s Mom and Learning What His Name Really Means at Long John Silver’s

Across films such as " Ghatashraddha " (1977), "Tabarana Kathe" (1986), "Thaayi Saheba" (1997), "Dweepa" (2002) and "Gulabi Talkies" (2008), Kasaravalli has kept returning to one question: how societies exclude individuals and communities, and how people who are themselves victims of oppressive structures can also become complicit in perpetuating them.

Asked whether the 1977 Kannada classic "Ghatashraddha," which examines religious orthodoxy and social exclusion, still spoke to contemporary India, Kasaravalli said: "All my films talk about othering. I always talk about how society looks at some people from a different lens, and in that process they make them 'other.'" He described this as "the biggest cruelty an individual or a group of people can impart on another person."

Asked whether he considered himself a political filmmaker, Kasaravalli said: "Whoever makes something, whether he makes mainstream cinema or art cinema, he is making a political statement, either in support of the dominant ideology or opposing the dominant ideology. He cannot avoid it." There is nothing called only entertainment, he added, and even entertainment is a political form. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

On his characters, he said: "I don't want any of my characters to become a kind of a mouthpiece to a certain ideology." Drawing on Jean-Luc Godard, he compared understanding a character to buying a house: one must examine it from the outside and then from within before making a judgment. Similarly, a filmmaker must inhabit a character and then step back to assess it. For Kasaravalli, characters are too complex for a filmmaker to easily take sides.

On the evolution of his cinematic language, Kasaravalli described the visual construction of "Ghatashraddha," as "ritualistic cinema." "The style is not imposed on it; it comes from within the content itself," he said. Since "Ghatashraddha" was about a ritual, he felt its cinematic form should reflect that structure.

Kasaravalli said he could not write a script until he had clarity about its images. "For me, the film is not merely making statements; it's an attempt by the filmmaker to impart an experience." He described writing detailed instructions for his crew, down to which hand a character uses to lift a glass, because even that changes the composition of a shot.

This attention to the relationship between character and environment shaped "Gulabi Talkies." Kasaravalli told cinematographer S. Ramachandra that the coastal community had to be as important as the protagonist. He wanted the images to feel like "actuality coverage," not a predetermined visual construction. Rejecting conventional scenic shots of the sea and rocks, he told his cinematographer: "Film should not have any pretty image." They chose 16mm, allowing the grain to contribute to the film's sense of actuality.

The discussion of visual aesthetics brought him to Cuban filmmaker Julio García Espinosa's idea of "imperfect cinema," which, for Kasaravalli, challenged the assumption that Western aesthetics should define cinematic perfection. "I don't want to take your aesthetic sensibility as my sensibility," he said, quoting Espinosa. Kasaravalli said each country and each region has its own aesthetic concerns. "We should make films according to that condition; we should never imitate the West. Why should I be perfect? I should be loyal to my own milieu."

Asked whether parallel cinema belonged to a particular period, Kasaravalli disagreed, pointing to notable films being made across the country today. The larger problem, he said, was reaching audiences. Of streaming platforms, he said: "We all thought it is going to be a solution for all of us. But OTT [streaming] is exactly doing what the mainstream distribution network was doing earlier." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In the audience Q&A, he addressed open endings and whether a filmmaker should provide answers. "A filmmaker who says that he knows answers for all the questions in life is telling a lie," he said. "He is also as confused as you are. He only throws up options so that you can start thinking. There is nothing called closure… life is always open."

As the session concluded, IFFI festival director Ashutosh Gowariker described Kasaravalli's work as "textbooks," saying he had returned to "Ghatashraddha" while developing a new film. He also singled out the filmmaker's close-ups. "You let your actors simply be. You make the audience think and anticipate what the character is going through," Gowariker said.

articles.title: What Is the Most Misunderstood '80s Sci-Fi Movie? There's a Clear Answer
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Orion Pictures I love a good science-fiction movie that gives you something to think about after the explosions stop. The 1980s had plenty of them, from Blade Runner to The Terminator. But there's one movie that seems to get remembered for all the wrong reasons. It's violent, occasionally ridiculous, and has a giant metal man who shoots […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google I love a good science-fiction movie that gives you something to think about after the explosions stop. The 1980s had plenty of them, from Blade Runner to The Terminator . But there's one movie that seems to get remembered for all the wrong reasons. It's violent, occasionally ridiculous, and has a giant metal man who shoots criminals in the face. What's not to love? Yet there's considerably more going on beneath all that mayhem. In fact, I think one of the decade's most entertaining sci-fi movies also happens to be one of its sharpest social satires.

Paul Verhoeven wasn't exactly interested in making another straightforward action movie. He had something much nastier in mind. His vision of the future was full of corporate greed, television sensationalism, and people who had apparently decided that everything was better when somebody could make money from it. There's also a surprisingly heartbreaking story hiding underneath the mechanical armor. And that's why I think RoboCop deserves another look.

Released in 1987, RoboCop introduced audiences to Alex Murphy, a Detroit police officer who gets brutally murdered by a gang led by Clarence Boddicker. His remains become the foundation for a new crime-fighting machine developed by Omni Consumer Products. The company wants to take over Detroit's police force and sees Murphy's transformation as a wonderful business opportunity. There's just one little problem. Murphy hasn't entirely disappeared. Memories of his former life begin returning, and the supposedly obedient machine starts looking rather inconvenient for the people who built him. Peter Weller does some terrific work here. He manages to make a character covered in metal feel like a real person struggling to understand what happened to him. That's not exactly easy when most of your face is hidden behind a futuristic helmet of a RoboCop . Check out this trailer and see for yourself.

Of course, Verhoeven also makes sure there's plenty of outrageous fun along the way. The commercials for bizarre products and the news reports about increasingly ridiculous disasters give the movie a wonderfully nasty sense of humor. Then there's the infamous demonstration of ED-209, which goes spectacularly wrong during a corporate presentation. It's one of the funniest scenes in the entire movie. But there's a reason these moments work so well. Verhoeven isn't just throwing random jokes into an action film. He's showing us a society where corporate executives treat human lives like another line on a balance sheet. The violence is deliberately excessive, and the humor makes the whole thing even more uncomfortable. RoboCop wants you to laugh.

The thing I find most interesting about RoboCop isn't actually the political satire. It's Murphy himself. Before the company turned him into a walking weapons platform, he was a husband, a father, and a police officer who thought he was doing something worthwhile. Now he's expected to follow instructions and protect a corporation's interests. His memories don't fit neatly into that arrangement. Watching Murphy slowly recover pieces of his identity gives the movie an emotional center that plenty of action films would have ignored. There's a particularly effective sadness to his attempts to remember his family. He can still recognize fragments of his old life, but he can't simply return to it. That's a pretty bleak idea for a movie that also features a giant robot shooting people during a boardroom presentation. Weller deserves a lot of credit for making both sides of the character work.

It's also worth remembering that RoboCop wasn't universally dismissed when it arrived. Roger Ebert gave it a positive review in 1987 and recognized the unusual combination of comedy, philosophy, and social commentary. Other critics struggled more with its mixture of genres and graphic violence. That confusion has largely disappeared as the movie's reputation has grown. Yet I still think people sometimes focus on the wrong things when discussing it. The film's corporate satire feels remarkably relevant, but its story about a man fighting to reclaim his humanity is what gives it staying power. Verhoeven would explore similar ideas in Total Recall and Starship Troopers , but there's something especially effective about the way he brings them together here. RoboCop may have been built like a big, noisy action movie. Underneath all that steel was a much sadder story. And that's the part I think deserves more attention.

And what do you guys think? Is this series really misunderstood? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title: Marvel Delivered Its Most Terrifying MCU Villain 11 Years Ago, And He Broke the TV Series That Created Him
articles.summary: The Marvel Cinematic Universe has had its fair share of impressive and imposing villains throughout its 18 years of existence. Killmonger had an understandable motivation and was so tough that he actually took over as Black Panther for a time. The High Evolutionary didn't care who or what he harmed to get what he wanted. […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The Marvel Cinematic Universe has had its fair share of impressive and imposing villains throughout its 18 years of existence. Killmonger had an understandable motivation and was so tough that he actually took over as Black Panther for a time. The High Evolutionary didn't care who or what he harmed to get what he wanted. Even the often heroic Wanda Maximoff proved to be a terrifying antagonist in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness . Of course, Thanos literally snapped away half of all life and defeated the Avengers. Despite all those villains, the scariest one in the history of the franchise debuted in 2015.

That antagonist is sometimes known as the Purple Man and he's the main villain for Jessica Jones to combat. The character was the focal point of the inaugural season of Jessica Jones on Netflix, which is often forgotten about by many people because it hasn't played a major part in the greater MCU. Outside of the titular character returning in Daredevil: Born Again , it hasn't mattered all that much. The Purple Man is also known as Kilgrave and he was so frightening that once he was gone, the show couldn't find that same level of success or quality.

If you looked at Kilgrave and knew nothing else about him, you wouldn't think he could be considered the MCU's scariest bad guy . Played by the incredibly talented David Tennant, Kilgrave looks like an everyday dude. He wears a suit, is relatively thin, and couldn't beat up most people. He's certainly no match for the powerful Jessica Jones from a physicality standpoint. What makes him so scary is his ability to control minds and make people do whatever he wants by simply telling them what to do. Taking away someone's agency is one of the most evil and scary things you could do.

Before we even see Kilgrave, we see the effects of his powers. He held Hope Shlottman captive, sexually abused her, and told her to kill her parents. When we actually see him (though not his face at this point), he takes over a family's house and forces them to do whatever he says. We also learn that he enslaved Jessica for a time in the past, using her for sex and whatever else he wanted. Kilgrave did this all without any remorse and didn't even see anything wrong with it. He believed that Jessica wanted to be with him, while she had suffered from PTSD after breaking away from him.

Every scene with Kilgrave was rife with tension. You always watched nervously, knowing that he could destroy lives in an instant. When he escapes Jessica's capture midway through Season 1, he tells Jessica's best friend Trish to shoot herself in the head. It's a terrifying scene that only has a somewhat happy ending because the gun was empty. Seeing Jessica, one of the strongest MCU heroes physically and mentally, showcase such a sense of fear around Kilgrave sold his villain status even more. Their dynamic helped make Jessica Jones Season 1 one of the best seasons of Marvel television ever produced.

Almost everyone who reads Jessica Jones comic books tends to agree that Kilgrave is her greatest enemy. The stories surrounding him and Jessica are so captivating that the comics ran into a problem where they couldn't quite deliver tales nearly as good without him. The Netflix series had the same trouble. While Season 1 of Jessica Jones was brilliant, the show couldn't find a villain anywhere near as compelling in the two following seasons. Season 2 was praised for the performances and the focus on female characters, but Jessica's mom returning never grabbed audiences the way Kilgrave did.

Jessica Jones Season 3 expanded on Trish's story and saw her utilize her enhanced abilities to become a vigilante. It also gave us an intense and highly intelligent psychopath as the villain, but as dangerous as he was, nothing really came close to how Kilgrave's scenes felt. In a lot of ways, Jessica Jones may have benefitted from starting with other villains before moving on to Kilgrave, as he's a nearly impossible act to follow, which the comics have proven. The fact that Kilgrave could be as scary as he was on a streaming service that saw Kingpin dominating screens at the same time is a testament to how chilling the character is.

As a whole, Jessica Jones is a very strong show. Krysten Ritter gave great performances over each episode, and while it was never bad, it certainly peaked during that first season. Kilgrave was a big part of that because the best thing you can do for a great superhero story is to give them someone absolutely terrifying to face off against. Kilgrave's ability to scare us without being physically imposing is something you felt in your bones and is something no other MCU villain can match.

Do you think there's a scarier MCU antagonist than Kilgrave? Let us know your picks in the comments.

articles.title: 3 Unadaptable Sci-Fi Books That Actually Became Great Movies (But One Took Multiple Attempts)
articles.summary: The label “unadaptable” has been slapped onto many works of literature over the years, especially in science fiction. Since the birth of the film industry in 1895, studios, producers, and filmmakers have been trying to film the unfilmable, finding creative ways to capture complex worlds and internal struggles with cinematic visuals. Historically, when someone attempts […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The label “unadaptable” has been slapped onto many works of literature over the years, especially in science fiction . Since the birth of the film industry in 1895, studios, producers, and filmmakers have been trying to film the unfilmable, finding creative ways to capture complex worlds and internal struggles with cinematic visuals. Historically, when someone attempts to adapt an “unadaptable” story, detractors, fans, and sometimes even the authors of the original works come out against the project, claiming it can’t be done.

But as the following films prove, telling Hollywood it can’t do something only adds fuel to the fire. Regardless of previous stalled projects or failed attempts, a visionary filmmaker eventually steps up to the plate, ready to take on the challenge. The result, at least in these cases, is a masterful mind-bending tale or sweeping science fiction odyssey that wows audiences in theaters and becomes a home-viewing classic that stands the test of time.

Watchmen began as a 12-issue comic series from DC, written by Alan Moore and illustrated by Dave Gibbons. But Moore himself argued that Watchmen wasn’t cinematic, noting that a comic reader can flip back and connect details, while film forces you to watch at 24 frames per second. Another problem was the scope. After Moore declined to write the screenplay, screenwriter Sam Hamm attempted to squeeze the 338-page comic into a 128-page script. When the project moved to Warner Bros., it attached sci-fi master Terry Gilliam, who was unhappy with Hamm’s script, bringing in Charles McKeown to rewrite it using Rorschach’s journal as voice-over. Although it seemed they’d gotten closer, Gilliam’s film also collapsed over budget, and later drafts by David Hayter replaced it.

Warner Bros. eventually hired director Zack Snyder in 2006, and the rest is history. Snyder pulled it off by using the comic itself as his storyboard. He added a title montage to explain the alternate history, and used a simplified ending taken from Hayter. Moore himself ultimately took no credit for the film and gave his share of the income to Gibbons. Gibbons said that watching it on DVD would feel like flipping through the book, since viewers could pause and rewind, and he was right: DVD sales are where Watchmen made its money back. Today, Watchmen is considered a superhero sci-fi classic, and it even launched a Watchmen sequel series from Damon Lindelof .

Philip K. Dick’s A Scanner Darkly entranced readers with the story of an undercover cop in a near-future world who gets involved with a dangerous new drug and begins to lose his identity. However, Dick’s writing is known for being extremely internal, leading readers through the breakdown of the protagonist’s perception from the inside; something nearly impossible to show visually on screen. Director Richard Linklater, who had experimented with rotoscoping on Waking Life , was interested in adapting one of Dick’s novels. He first played around with Ubik , but eventually turned to A Scanner Darkly , deciding to direct it as an intimate animated sci-fi thriller, made for only $8.7 million. His script followed the novel closely, and when he pitched it to Dick’s estate, it was approved.

It was ultimately Linklater’s rotoscoped animation that was key to the film’s success. The technique involved filming live actors (including Keanu Reeves, Robert Downey Jr., Woody Harrelson, and Winona Ryder), then having animators paint over the footage frame by frame. The result is a shifting, dreamlike animation that conveys the character’s fragmented, drug-induced perception while still allowing the actors to give live performances. Instead of turning it into a big-budget action thriller, Linklater leaned into the story's internal nature, helming what is now considered not only a cult classic, but one of the more successful Dick adaptations and one of Linklater’s most unique films.

Frank Herbert’s space opera opus Dune built out an entire galaxy’s politics, theology, ecology, and characters. The first notable adaptation attempt came when director Alejandro Jodorowsky began plotting his film, which included music by Pink Floyd and a dream cast of Orson Welles, Salvador Dalí, and Mick Jagger. Trouble was, Jodorowsky’s script would have made a 14-hour movie, and he’d already spent $2 million of the $9 million budget on pre-production. Thus, the project stalled. Next, Ridley Scott was hired to direct and was the first to consider splitting the book into two films. However, Scott’s version focused on an incestuous relationship, which outraged Herbert, and Scott ultimately dropped the project to make Blade Runner . David Lynch then became the first to put the book on screen, though he famously didn’t get final cut, and the result was so disastrous that Lynch disowned the film.

Enter modern-day sci-fi master Denis Villeneuve. Following the idea Scott first floated, he split the story into two films. Using minimal dialogue, he relied on largely practical visual world-building and took a restrained approach to adapting the story and characters, leaving the audience to build out much of the world for themselves without over-explaining the complicated lore and terminology. His adaptations have finally proven a success, making the unfilmable filmable, with Dune: Part Two making over $714 million worldwide. His upcoming Dune: Part Three , based on the next novel, Dune Messiah , is set to open in December as the final film in the trilogy.

Are there any sci-fi novels you think are truly unfilmable? Let us know in the comments below.

articles.title: A Forgotten Sci-Fi Series About a Detective in a Time Loop Premiered 20 Years Ago, And It Deserves a Reboot
articles.summary: There was a time when television commercials and television drama boldly embraced the bizarre. Before the days of streamed TV shows and endless murder mysteries with devious plots, there were the networks, which occasionally dared to take oddball plots and turn them into unexpected detective hits. This series asked: What if every choice you made […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google There was a time when television commercials and television drama boldly embraced the bizarre. Before the days of streamed TV shows and endless murder mysteries with devious plots, there were the networks, which occasionally dared to take oddball plots and turn them into unexpected detective hits. This series asked: What if every choice you made could end your life? That's enough to be exhausting on its own. Now, try to work through a murder mystery while keeping that in mind.

It's exactly the kind of perfectly warped conceit that helped turn an underrated ABC thriller into a fully realized series. It was filled with nonstop action, intrigue, and a twisting conspiracy. But unfortunately, the lead actor was underused and underappreciated in his role. Then, the show somehow slipped through the cracks before it could be appreciated by an audience that never knew what to fully make of it. Twenty years later, it's time to re-explore its ideas.

When it premiered on November 15, 2006, Day Break showcased Taye Diggs as Detective Brett Hopper, a Los Angeles cop caught up in the murder of Assistant District Attorney Alberto Garza. Doggedly convinced that he's innocent of the crime, Hopper faces the uphill climb of trying to prove it. When he wakes up after the shooting, he discovers that he's living the same day over again… only with his previous memories intact. As the days pass, Hopper finds himself reliving the same day, remembering every arrest, every altercation, and every bruise from his previous attempts.

The brilliance of Day Break is how it combines the Groundhog Day setup with the frenzied pacing of a 24 -type conspiracy thriller . Hopper can't just sit there and wait until the next day, because the next day isn't coming. He has to traverse his current reality and save himself from getting framed, while doing everything he can to save his loved ones. And he's doing it on a timetable that's getting out of control. As it turns out, being able to foresee the future doesn't make life any easier, because saving one person might get another person killed, and fixing one thing means creating ten more. The clever way in which Day Break complicates an already difficult day makes this show a jewel.

Unfortunately, Day Break was never able to build the audience that its bold premise deserved. ABC was all too quick to place the series in the prized Wednesday night time slot that was previously occupied by Lost and meant to make the show highly visible. But ABC quickly pulled it from the lineup, dumping it after only a handful of episodes had aired in December 2006. Luckily, the remainder of the episodes were eventually made available online, so fans could follow Hopper's terrifying quest to its natural conclusion. The first season was only 13 episodes long, but the creators of the series had planned for many more exciting seasons, where instead of having Hopper relive the same day over and over, they could have him stumble into completely new conspiracies and impossible situations.

It's an enticing prospect. In the original series, viewers experienced the unique storytelling opportunity of watching a detective remember events that everyone else experienced as if they were happening for the first time. A reboot could go in any number of directions and still land close to the original's exciting combination of action, mystery, and romance. Taye Diggs made Brett Hopper thoroughly sympathetic, anchoring even the wildest of situations. There are dozens of television shows about detectives in pursuit of killers, but how many give their hero the chance to learn from the same terrible day again? Day Break had a truly clever premise, and 20 years later, it's a premise worth revisiting. Sometimes a show with a great concept goes to waste before it has a chance to take off.

If television keeps bringing back the same old detective stories, perhaps it's time to give one that literally repeated itself another shot. After all, even a show trapped in a time loop deserves a second chance! Would you bring Day Break back for another season, or do you think its time has finally run out? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title: Toy Story Franchise Future Addressed by Pixar, And It's the Right Call
articles.summary: IMAGE COURTESY OF PIXAR The future of Toy Story remains open. That, at least, is according to producer Lindsey Collins, speaking to Deadline's Anthony D'Allesandro. It may seem obvious that that's how Pixar has been looking at it, but now we have confirmation. After having a perfect ending to the second film…then the third…then the fourth, the Pixar brain […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The future of Toy Story remains open. That, at least, is according to producer Lindsey Collins, speaking to Deadline's Anthony D'Allesandro. It may seem obvious that that's how Pixar has been looking at it, but now we have confirmation. After having a perfect ending to the second film…then the third…then the fourth, the Pixar brain trust have realized that it's just better to never say never. There is, however, a suggestion that the franchise could break into sub-trilogies. Characters never need age in cartoons, but they have in the Toy Story movies, with Andy moving on from the toys at the end of Toy Story 3 .

Collins suggests, therefore, that it's possible a sixth film could wrap up a "Bonnie trilogy," but likely wouldn't put an end to the toys. Even actors aging out doesn't stop the characters, as Jim Varney and Don Rickles have passed on as the years went along, and their characters recast with sound-alikes. Take a look at the relevant interview snippet below:

Could there be a 'Toy Story 6?' Does Pixar have plans for more sequels? Hear what producer Lindsey Collins told us ⬇️ See more from #DeadlineContenders Film: Los Angeles here: https://t.co/R0EvkHzn6Z pic.twitter.com/YQ7K3CyGs1

The premise of Toy Story is everlasting as long as kids like toys. That, however, is a proposition more in jeopardy nowadays than ever before. Basic action figures from Star Wars or superhero comics now run $20-$30 — a talking doll like Woody would be at least $50, and an electronic deluxe figure with action features like Buzz Lightyear would be $100 minimum. They're no longer buyable with a basic allowance, and if it's a choice between an open-world video game with days of gameplay versus one talking figure, guess what kids are going to get first? Oil prices and tariffs get blamed, but even when those get better, toy price raises never go back down.

The Toy Story movies, especially the newest one, deal with this issue. Plushes should always be affordable; toy bricks like LEGO are costly, but do make small, cheaper sets for all budgets. Change the protagonists, and you can make infinite (and beyond?) Toy Story movies. If they're to be about Woody and Buzz Lightyear specifically, though, we live in a time when, increasingly, only adults would buy and collect similar items. Such adults have typically been villains in the series, which advocates for playing with playthings. Yet some adult collectors "play" too, via toy photography and stop-motion videos. Would your kids want to see a movie about them, though?

It's been an impressive run, regardless. The first Toy Story came out in 1995, 31 years ago, and was the first feature length, fully CG animated film. Tom Hanks was one of the biggest stars in the world, and Tim Allen had just successfully moved from a top-rated sitcom into movies with The Santa Clause . All these years later, both men are still household names, though the toys they voiced might be even better known around the world. Over the years, the sequels have added even more beloved characters, from Jessie and Bullseye to Forky and Duke Caboom . As long as we have filmmakers who grew up playing with toys, the possibilities remain as boundless as a child's imagination. When today's kids grow up…we'll see.

Do you think Toy Story should plan a definitive ending, or is it best to just run with good ideas when and if they come? Buzz into comments and light up our boards with your thoughts.

articles.title: One Piece’s Elbaph Arc Teases Luffy Is One Step Closer to Gear 6
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Toei Animation Warning: This article contains spoilers from the One Piece manga! Luffy's powers continue to grow in the ongoing Elbaph Arc. It's been over two years since One Piece entered the second arc of the Final Saga, and the situation hasn't been worse than this. It didn't take long for Elbaph to turn into a battlefield […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Warning: This article contains spoilers from the One Piece manga! Luffy's powers continue to grow in the ongoing Elbaph Arc. It's been over two years since One Piece entered the second arc of the Final Saga, and the situation hasn't been worse than this. It didn't take long for Elbaph to turn into a battlefield when the Holy Knights arrived there with the intention of making them bend to Imu's will. The World Government has been eyeing the power of the strongest race, and they don't plan on waiting longer now that the war is upon them. After seeing that the Holy Knights may not be able to accomplish their goals, Imu descended on the island and finally revealed his true appearance.

The mysterious ruler of the world is even more powerful than fans imagined, which just proves the gap in power between him and Luffy. Luffy has been on a whole other level ever since he awakened his Devil Fruit in Wano. His Gear 5 comes with incredible powers , but the drawbacks make it impossible for him to defeat powerful opponents effortlessly. However, as the fight against Imu continues, Luffy taps into his mysterious powers that may hint at his true awakening or his Gear 6 form.

For some time, fans believed that Gear 5 is truly the peak of his powers because of what he said in Wano during his awakening. Luffy never felt this powerful before, which is all the more reason why he called his awakening his “peak.” Luffy managed to overpower Kaido and save Wano, but that was only the beginning. The series introduced the limitations related to Gear 5, and the Egghead Island Arc made it clear that Luffy isn't powerful enough to defeat the major villains.

Things became even worse in Elbaph when Imu effortlessly stabbed him even when he was in his Gear 5 form. This near-death situation again caused Luffy to tap into a new level of power. Luffy awakened his Gear 5 in a similar way after he was fatally injured in Wano. However, this time, instead of another awakening, Luffy revealed a new form that shifts into a more feral, monkey-like state that giants refer to as Dark Nika in motifs. The series hasn't officially dubbed this form as Gear 6, and the true abilities of Luffy in this form are still unknown.

However, this is most likely the first step towards him unlocking the true potential of his Devil Fruit. After meeting Luffy, Imu knew that he was nowhere near the level of Joyboy, which was yet another hint that the young pirate hasn't unlocked all his powers yet. Luffy's Devil Fruit is as mysterious as it is whimsical. It allows him to turn imagination into reality and transform into something of a mythical being. Even so, without truly understanding his own powers, he will never be able to defeat the big shots, especially Imu.

The reason why Luffy achieving a Gear 6 is more crucial than ever is because of the drawbacks of his Gear 5 form. While combining his Devil Fruit powers with Haki, his stamina drains instantly, something the series already revealed in Dressrosa when his Gear 4 form was introduced. However, this problem became even more evident with his Gear 5, especially since whenever Luffy drains his stamina, he starts looking like an old man who can’t even lift a finger. The only way he can get back into fighting is by filling his stomach and getting his energy back, which takes time.

The battles are already intense, and it gets even more impossible for others to buy him enough time to replenish his energy. This happened to him several times in Egghead, and he keeps running into the same problem all over again. At this rate, his Gear 5 form is only good enough to defeat opponents like Rob Lucci or anyone weak enough so Luffy can deal with them in just a few blows. However, when faced against the Five Elders, Holy Knights, and even Imu, Luffy needs much more power than he realizes.

Do you think One Piece is setting up the stage for Luffy's Gear 6? What kind of powers do you think he can unlock next? Share your thoughts in the comments below.

articles.summary: Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond, ending a multi-year search for actor Daniel Craig's replacement. Of course, during his five-film run as Bond (over the course of 15 years), there were several moments with Craig where it looked like he might drop out. That sparked many discussions, fairly early on, about […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond , ending a multi-year search for actor Daniel Craig's replacement. Of course, during his five-film run as Bond (over the course of 15 years), there were several moments with Craig where it looked like he might drop out. That sparked many discussions, fairly early on, about who should play the next 007, and one name that circulated for years was Idris Elba.

Talk of Elba playing Bond really heated up in the 2010s, but for every who supported the idea, there was another who was dead set against Elba breaking the barrier to become the first black Bond. Elba eventually recused himself from the discussion after going through years of backlash, and is probably one of the happiest people on the planet that the next Bond has been cast, and the discussion can end.

Idris Elba is starring in the new survival thriller Above the Below, which he also co-directs with Martin Owen. The film combines nightmare scenarios of both space travel and sea travel, into a story where a trio of astronauts have their capsule veer off course and crash land into the ocean upon re-entry to Earth. With no communications and no sure way to know if anyone knows their location to send help, the trio must figure out how to survive on their own in the high-pressure situation.

During the press junket for Above the Below , ComicBook's Chris Killian checked in with Idris Elba about the Bond casting. More importantly, he made sure Elba new that there are actual gambling sites that are now placing him as a major frontrunner bet to play a Bond villain. So, is that flattering to Elba, or is this the resurgence of a conversation he really wanted to stop having? You already know the answer:

"Flattered? Yeah! I mean, what a compliment. You know, only because it's, like, one of the most charismatic characters in the world [Bond]. But, yeah, I am flattered."

Most fans would point out that Idris Elba kinda, sorta, has already played a Bond(esque) villain character in the Fast & Furious spinoff film, Hobbs & Sha w. However, we would argue that the actor's scenery-devouring performance in that film (delivering all-time classic lines like "I'm Black Superman!") is a far cry from what he would bring to the table as an antagonist in the shadowy espionage world of spies and assassins that James Bond operates in. As usual, Elba is the full package: a fitting pick for a villain who is both a physical threat and has the dramatic gravitas of a great mastermind foe. Seeing him dip into something a little more eccentric, as so many other Bond villain actors have, would also be a delight for fans. Plus, Idris Elba working with new Bond director Denis Villeneuve ( Dune trilogy) is a pairing we'd love to see, and is long overdue.

Having Idris Elba anywhere near the James Bond franchise, in any capacity, would be a win. Here's hoping those betting odds are ever in his favor. Above the Below will be released on December 4th. Bond 26 is in production and expected in 2028.

articles.title: Blade Director Reveals the Major Problems Behind Scrapped MCU Movie, And the Big Lesson It Taught Him
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Director Bassam Tariq revealed why the Blade movie never got made, and it all came down to bad scripts. One of the biggest disappointments from the Marvel Cinematic Universe is the fact that Marvel Studios couldn't get the Blade movie made, even with a two-time Oscar winner signed on to play the lead role. Even […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Director Bassam Tariq revealed why the Blade movie never got made, and it all came down to bad scripts. One of the biggest disappointments from the Marvel Cinematic Universe is the fact that Marvel Studios couldn't get the Blade movie made, even with a two-time Oscar winner signed on to play the lead role. Even star Mahershala Ali said he couldn't believe it never got made, and MCU head honcho Kevin Feige called it his biggest failure, a statement that Ali agreed with . However, with the blame game going around, Tariq has told his side of the story, and it explains why he felt he needed to step away from the production.

In an interview with The New Arab , Tariq said that the movie was not being made the right way. “It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script,” Tariq said. "You’re sitting there and explaining to actors what their role will be, and they just have to believe you. That’s also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn’t add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot. All I have is my integrity, and I’ve been thinking about that a lot."

Bassam Tariq said that he was hired to be the Blade movie director , and he had to keep telling his actors, including Mahershala Ali, what they would be doing in the movie. However, he never got a completed script that was satisfactory, and it meant he kept having to give bad news to the actors when it wasn't even Tariq's fault. He went on to say that all the decisions were coming from a corporate entity, and that is not a good place to be in as a movie director.

Tariq then said that he was losing credibility with the actors and it wasn't a healthy way to have a career as a movie director. He then bluntly said why he wanted to leave the Blade movie when he realized how the production was going. "Life’s too short to make shit films," he said. He went on to say the one thing he learned from working on Blade was that he has to have full control over his script. He then said if there are disagreements, they are between them and him. He finished by saying that it was sad because they had high hopes for the movie that they wanted to make.

According to Variety , Blade was passed around to five different writers while it was in development. This included names like Stacy Osei-Kuffour (Watchmen) and Michael Starrbury. After Tariq left the production, Yann Demange signed on to direct it, but the movie never got made. Ali is no longer connected to the role, and he has moved on . There is now no Blade movie in the works, although there is a chance Blade could get recast and added to something like a possible Midnight Sons big-screen movie following the 2028 Ghost Rider release.

Carroll, an actor who starred in The Punisher and had a voice role in Grand Theft Auto V , has died. He was 66 years old. According to Deadline , the actor died suddenly while en route to a voice-over booking. His rep, Jon Mason of Mason-Lewis Entertainment, did not provide a cause of death. Information about survivors or a memorial service was not made available.

For Marvel fans, Carroll is best known for his role as Doctor Charles in the Netflix series The Punisher . For video game fans, he is best known for his voice role in the 2013 release of Grand Theft Auto V , where he was the voice of The Local Population. These are just two of several roles that Carroll took on over his long career in Hollywood, where he had parts in some successful TV shows and some major movies as well.

Carroll was born in 1960, and he has an almost three-decade career in movies, television, video games, and more. He got his first break in Hollywood in 1998 with a role as a cop on an episode of Law & Order . From there, he appeared in the Law & Order franchise, appearing on several different episodes of the various franchise shows. This was where he got his start and how his career progressed over the years. However, he also had a chance in the 2000s to appear in some movies by some big-name directors.

In 2009, he earned a role in the Darren Aronofsky movie The Wrestler , which starred Mickey Rourke as a past-his-prime professional wrestler trying to stay in the spotlight. He also appeared in The Cake Eaters, The Capers, The Winning Season, The Hungry Ghosts, A Fish Story , and Everything's Fine . He also returned to television, where he got a role in two episodes of Boardwalk Empire , the HBO crime drama that starred Steve Buscemi. He also took roles in several more shows in the 2010s, including The Blacklist , Blue Bloods , High Maintenance , Pose , and Marvel's Netflix series The Punisher .

This all led to his biggest role, starring as Fat Mooney on HBO's The Deuce . Fat was a man who ran a New York City sex shop that was owned by the show's lead character, Frankie Martino (James Franco). This was his most extended role, as he appeared in six episodes of the series that followed the rise of the New York porn industry.

One of his final roles came in A Delicate Arrangement , a movie that is coming out by director Nick Sandow. It stars Carla Gugino as Vivien Leigh in the true story of the two-time Oscar-winning actress’s relationship with a Philadelphia florist (Matthew Modine). Carroll also voiced a character in the blockbuster 2013 video game Grand Theft Auto and played Dr. Scott in The Rocky Horror Tribute Show .

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google There is a new series of books from Marvel about battles between worlds during the "Time Runs Out" event that the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday movie is based on. As a reminder, "Time Runs Out" was a storyline that ran in the pages of New Avengers and The Avengers where the incursions were starting to destroy all the Earths in the multiverse. They happened when two Earths appeared in space together, and after a few hours, they would collide, destroying them both. Doctor Strange found a way to save some of the worlds, and that seems to be the basis of the first book in this new run, X-Men Incursions .

X-Men Incursions #1 (2026) by Alex Paknadel and Jim Towe brought together two of the X-Men's most famous alternate worlds in an incursion event. These were Earth-811, the "Days of Future Past" world, and Earth-58163, the "House of M" world . As with all incursions, either both worlds will die, or one will be saved. In this case, there was no battle between the worlds, and Doctor Strange held their fate in his hands.

This issue didn't have the two worlds battle each other, although there was a crossover. The Sentinels on Earth-811 were fighting Kate Pryde and Carol Danvers, but they stopped when they detected more mutants on the orbiting Earth, and they left to attack the mutants on Earth-58163. Right after the Sentinels left, the Black Priests showed up. When Kate Pryde was trying to figure out what was happening, Doctor Strange revealed himself alongside the Black Priests. Now, it might be time to remind readers of who this group is.

In "Time Runs Out," Doctor Doom accidentally started the incursions when he traveled through time and space to kill every version of the Molecule Man there was because he realized the Beyonders were going to use all the Molecule Men as a bomb to destroy the multiverse. However, when he began killing all of the Molecule Men, it started the first incursions by destabilizing those worlds. That led Doctor Strange to join and lead the Black Priests and to eventually work with Doctor Doom to save the multiverse from the new threat.

When the worlds were about to collide, several things could happen, and one of these was the Black Priests' arrival. Doctor Strange used dark magic to lead the Black Priests to intrusive Earths in an attempt to stop the incursions and save the multiverse. In this case, they showed up on Earth-811 and began to do their work. While this was happening, Doctor Strange took Kate Pryde on a journey to Earth-58163.

The Black Priests worked to stabilize the multiverse by choosing an Earth to destroy, and this issue showed how Doctor Strange reached that decision. Earth-58163 and Earth-811 could not have been any more different. In "Days of Future Past," Sentinels ruled the planet and either killed or captured all mutants. The robots also killed regular heroes and took over rule from the government, which couldn't control them anymore. It was a dystopian nightmare. "House of M" was the perfect world that the Scarlet Witch created, where mutants were the ruling class, and everyone lived in peace. It was a utopian society, although one that wasn't completely right.

In X-Men Incursions , Kate Pryde accidentally killed Carol Danvers when she phased her into concrete after a blast ruined her concentration. The original "Days of Future Past" saw Wolverine, Colossus, and more die, and Kate was one of the few remaining survivors. Even her best friend, Rachel Summers, ended up traveling back in time, and Kate had nothing left to live for. Doctor Strange showed Kate Earth-58163, where she was a teacher, Wolverine and Nightcrawler were still fighting the good fight, and Carol Danvers was the world's greatest hero.

In "House of M," Wolverine fought to prove that this world was wrong because he knew it was better to live in the real world than in a product of Wanda Maximoff's imagination. On Earth-58163, since timelines only change when these things happen, it showed a world that was still living in peace, where mutants like Kate Pryde were living their best lives. Doctor Strange realized that "Days of Future Past" was a horrific timeline , and that was how he decided that "House of M," for all its problems, was always the Earth that needed to live on.

What are your thoughts on the battle between "Days of Future Past" and the "House of M" Earths in X-Men Incursions ? Let us know in the comments what battles you want to see next in this new Marvel comic line of stories.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google A 14-year-old PC game was the #1 best-selling Steam game for the week of November 10 to November 17, beating the likes of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , Phantom Blade Zero , Bodycam , and more. The Steam game in question recently got new DLC on November 10, and is also 75% off. This combo no doubt has contributed to its spike in sales, but it's still very impressive to see it atop the Steam charts well over a decade later.

Coming in at #10 for this week was the October-released indie game Moon Sweepers , which has been in the top 10 since its release. Meanwhile, in the #9 spot is Crimson Desert , which has returned to the top 10 for the first time in a while. In the #8 and #7 spots are actually DLC for the game in question. In the #6 spot is the September-released EA Sports FC 27 , which has also been in the top 10 since its release. The first game in the top five, in the #5 spot, is the new release Football Manager 27 . #4 is Phantom Blade Zero, which went #1 back at its launch at the end of October . Shooting up the charts into the #3 spot from far down is 2024's Bodycam. Lastly, the #2 game for the week was Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, which has been #1 every week since its release, except at the launch of Phantom Blade Zero , when it was briefly dethroned. Now, it's been dethroned again, this time by Euro Truck Simulator 2 . The aforementioned DLCs that also charted are the Coaches DLC and the larger Iceland DLC, both of which were released on November 12 and November 10, respectively.

One of the Best-Rated Games on Steam For those unfamiliar with Euro Truck Simulator 2 , it is a trucking simulator game, as its name suggests. Also, as its name implies, it's a sequel to 2008's Euro Truck Simulator . Developed and published by SCS Software, it is quietly very popular, which is why it has over 148,000 user reviews to date. More than that, it has a 97% approval rating across this massive number of reviews, which is wildly impressive. This gives the PC game an "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating on the Valve platform, the highest rating possible.

For those on the Steam Deck, and thus curious, Euro Truck Simulator 2 is Steam Deck Verified. This means Valve has tested the game on its PC handheld and can confirm it works from start to finish and works well, though the guarantee of the latter is not as consistent as many Steam Deck users would like. As for the aforementioned discount that brings the game down from $20 to $5, it is live until November 24.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Avatar: Seven Havens wrapped up its first season at the end of last month, leaving behind several burning questions. This is the first animation series of the franchise in 12 years, and there's no doubt the wait was worth it. The latest installment earned praise from fans and critics for its exceptional worldbuilding and captivating characters. The series premiered in October and ended in the same month after releasing the episodes in batches. The story centers around twin Earthbender sisters, Pavi and Nisha, as they navigate a world where the Avatar is feared among the masses rather than being treated as a savior.

The finale of Book 1 features Pavi heading off to the next Haven while Nisha decides to stay behind in Allora with Karthik. This helps the franchise set up the overarching journey for the upcoming seasons, which means fans are in for a new adventure. There are still a lot of things the story needs to resolve in the second season, but so far, there hasn’t been much information on the story. This is especially the case since the series hasn't yet revealed a trailer or even a teaser. Regardless, here are three things we have to see in Avatar: Seven Havens Season 2 .

Since the story takes place 225 years after the Legend of Korra , it's evident she is dead in Seven Havens but the exact circumstances of her death hasn't been revealed yet. Since humanity blames Korra for the cataclysm, Avatars are now feared in the world because of the terrifying abilities they possess. The first season only began to scratch through the surface of what led her to destroy the world with cataclysm.

Less than a week ago, executive producer Sehaj Sethi took part in a Reddit AMA and answered all sorts of fan questions about the upcoming season. She also confirmed fans will learn more about Korra and everything that led her to cause the cataclysm. Korra has been one of the major characters in the franchise, which is all the more reason fans are curious to see the truth behind the tragedy.

The first ends with the twin sisters being separated since they choose different paths for herslef. Unlike Pavi, heads toward the Floating Isles to unlock her next Chakra, Niska plans to help people while staying in the city. Their relationship fractured after the truth about their parents and Pavi's injury came out, which is all the more reason why the show needs to reunite them so they can confront their guilt, trauma, and resentment with each other.

The finale suggests that the twins might be separated for a time long time. However, with Sehaj Sethi confirming in an interview with IGN that there won't be a time-skip, we can expect the sisters to be reunited sooner than expected. There were several fan theories regarding a time-skip, which Sehaj debunked not long after the finale. Of course, that doesn't confirm the show will never have a time-skip, but at least we know nothing has been decided so far.

Before their renuion could happen, the twin sisters need to deal with their emotional conflict on their own, all the while staying on the path they have decided to follow. Pavi is traveling to the Floatng Isles to unlock her remaining chakra, especially since she saw a vision in the cosmic void after she unlocked her root chakra. On the other hand, Nisha aims to be recognized as the Avatar and change the public's perception after the tragedy that took place 225 years ago.

She also needs to deal with her childhood trauma and guilt when her fear of being abandoned by her parents caused her to have a fear-driven outburst, accidentally killing them and causing Pavi to lose the lower part of her left leg. Unlike Pavi, Nisha's chakras are open and surging with energy, which means her immediate challenge is controlling her raw power.

What are you most excited to see in Avatar: Seven Havens Season 2? What do you hope will happen next in the lives of Pavi and Nisha? Share your thoughts in the comments below!

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Sterling K. Brown, whom you may not have remembered as N'Jobu from the beginning of Black Panther , will face off against Nicolas Cage's creepiest character in recent memory in the next Longlegs movie. That's going to be quite a trick, because Cage's Longlegs died in the first film. Since he might have been in league with Satan, though, there are many possibilities in play. Deadline, which broke the story , says "it is not a straight sequel," and Maika Monroe's protagonist, Agent Lee Harper, is not expected to return. Chalk this up as a new potential franchise for Skydance, as Paramount has acquired the sequel rights from Neon.

Osgood Perkins returns as director, and it's unknown what Brown will be doing it. Since Longlegs is, shall we say, antisocial at best, the likelihood is that he'll be going against the pale-faced, high-voiced villain. The Longlegs character was spoofed by Chris Elliott in the recent Scary Movie re-quel , cementing the fact that it made enough of a pop culture footprint for horror fans to get the joke.

After years of stage roles and TV spots, Brown had his big acting breakthrough playing Christopher Darden on American Crime Story: The People Vs. OJ Simpson . Since then he has taken on a wide range of roles, from voicing Garry in The Angry Birds Movie 2 to being Oscar nominated for Best Supporting Actor for American Fiction . He continues to do both prestige and populist projects — he recently appeared in Cathy Yan's The Gallerist , and wrapped his role as arch-villain Zarkon in Rawson Marshall Thurber's Voltron movie.

Cage, known for making interesting acting choices when the director and script permit, based the Longlegs character on the androgynous guru in Fellini's Juliet of the Spirits , and the hand gestures and voice his mother used to use to try to lull him to sleep, inadvertently scaring him instead. It's a memorable enough character to spawn a horror franchise, though Cage doesn't often do sequels . Indeed, he said he was glad Spider-Noir got canceled in a way that completed the story arc , but left people wanting more and didn't overstay its welcome.

Cage often make big choices, but many of his most iconic roles depend on equally formidable costars. Holly Hunter in Raising Arizona . Elisabeth Shue in Leaving Las Vegas . Sean Connery in The Rock . And of course, Brendan Gleeson in Spider-Noir . Brown's best acting is often reacting, to Jeffrey Wright in American Fiction , or Sarah Paulson in The People vs. OJ Simpson . Putting the two together seems like a recipe for fireworks onscreen. Perkins, who has an unusual sensibility of his own, has a chance to really work some magic here. Depending, of course, on how credible in-universe he manages to make Longlegs' return. Will he take the Saw route and just rely on flashbacks within flashbacks? Or go the Jason route and simply have the man be unkillable? Fans of all involved surely can't wait to find out, but they have more than a year to wait. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Grand Theft Auto VI is a tremendous success, and it beat the entire box office run of Avengers: Endgame in less than 24 hours. As we previously reported, GTA 6 has already sold over 32.5 million copies pre-release. It was already known that it would be a huge hit, but the amount of sales has blown away anything that anyone expected. It not only set a new record for a video game launch, but it also proved that GTA is the biggest and most popular entertainment franchise, regardless of the medium. This includes movies, and it beat one of the most successful movies of all time in just one day.

Avengers: Endgame was released in 2019, and in its time in theaters, the movie made $2.9 billion. That makes it the highest-grossing movie of all time, passing Avatar thanks to the recent Avengers: Endgame Encore re-release . Even with the re-release and the original box office run, it has made almost a billion less than GTA 6 after just one day. With its 32.5 million copies, Grand Theft Auto VI has made $3.79 billion in sales on day one.

Even With All Other Variables, This Is a Big Win for Grand Theft Auto 6 Image Courtesy of Rockstar There could be arguments about how these are apples and oranges, but the truth is that Grand Theft Auto VI is clearly a bigger success than the highest-grossing movies in history. Even if all the rentals, digital sales, and physical copies that Avengers: Endgame has accounted for are included, there is almost no chance that it was enough to match what GTA 6 has made in just one day. However, the one argument that people could make is based on the cost of the entertainment.

Anyone who bought GTA 6 paid $79.99 for the Standard Edition and $99.99 for the Ultimate Edition. The average ticket price for movies in 2019 was around $9.16. At $2.9 billion, that means there were about 316.5 million tickets sold, which is much higher than the 32.5 million copies sold. But there is also the fact that people went to see Avengers: Endgame multiple times, and for GTA 6 , these are people buying the game once and owning it after that, although there might be more money made for the next GTA Online experience. Again, it's apples and oranges when looking at the two titles.

Even saying that, realizing that Grand Theft Auto VI made more money in its first day of sales than Avengers: Endgame made in its entire run shows how popular this video game property is. Beating out the most popular movie in the most successful movie franchise so quickly proves that fans were anxiously awaiting the release of the game, and those sales are just getting started.

What are your thoughts on Grand Theft Auto VI's quick sales? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.
